questions.title: Roll out a new prompt without betting the product on it
questions.prompt: A new version of a chat prompt looks better in a notebook. Design how it reaches users: the stages, how users are assigned, what you measure at each stage, and when it rolls back automatically.
questions.short: Run it in shadow first, on all traffic, logging its answers without showing them, and compare quality metrics with the current prompt. Then route a small share of users to it, 10% in the lesson, and widen in steps to 25%, 50% and 100% while the metrics hold. Assign by a deterministic hash of the user id so each user sees one version, and roll back automatically when the new version's error rate reaches twice the old one over a window of requests.
questions.full:
### Shadow mode

The new prompt runs on 100% of traffic but only its logs are kept. Nobody sees its output. This gives a full comparison of latency, cost per request, guardrail block rate and quality scores against the current version, and users never see a shadow answer. Shadow calls can share the provider quota with live calls, so give them a separate quota or key; otherwise a quota limit can slow or fail live requests. It is the same first stage that the ML design lesson calls shadow deployment for a model.

### Percentage rollout

Route 10% of traffic to the new version. If quality holds, raise it to 25%, then 50%, then 100%. If quality drops, switch back at once. Both versions stay deployed and the switch is configuration, so a rollback takes minutes, which is the lesson's rule for every stage.

### Deterministic assignment

Hash the user id combined with the name of the experiment and take it modulo 100. Buckets below the traffic share get the variant, the rest get the control. A user then sees the same version across requests inside one experiment, and the assignment can be recomputed later from the log. Random assignment per request mixes versions inside one conversation and makes the comparison noisy.

### What to measure

Per prompt version: latency percentiles, user ratings where they exist, error rate, guardrail block rate and cost per request. The eval logger records the template name and version with every request, so the metrics split by version without extra plumbing.

### Automatic rollback

The lesson's exercise sets the rule: when a new version shows 2x the error rate of the previous version over 100 requests, revert automatically. The window matters; a handful of requests is noise, and waiting for thousands lets a bad prompt run too long.

### A note on the business metric

Shadow and canary protect the user. Whether the new prompt improves the outcome that matters, such as task completion, needs a randomized split with enough traffic and time, which is the A/B stage from the ML design lesson.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why hash the user id and not pick randomly per request? Expected: a user then gets one consistent version across a session and the assignment is reproducible from the log.
- **Level 2:** What does shadow mode not tell you? Expected: how users react to the new answers; it only compares logged outputs and system metrics.
- **Level 3:** The new prompt costs more per request but scores higher. Who decides? Expected: a guardrail on cost per request decides whether it can ship at all; the quality gain against the cost is then a product decision with both numbers on the table.
- **Level 3:** How do you keep the control and the variant from sharing a cache entry? Expected: include the prompt version in the cache key, otherwise a hit returns the other version's answer and the comparison is corrupted.
questions.wrong:
- "Ship to everyone and watch the dashboard." A regression then hits every user before the dashboard moves.
- "Assign per request at random for a cleaner statistic." Users see both versions in one conversation and the logged metrics mix them.
- "Shadow mode is enough; skip the canary." Shadow mode never shows the output to a user, so it cannot measure user reaction.

questions.title: Batch or online serving for a two-hour freshness limit
questions.prompt: A feed ranking score must be no more than two hours old for 5,000,000 items, and the serving peak is 120 requests per second. Price batch and online serving with the lesson's cost model, pick one, and say what would flip the choice.
questions.short: With a one-hour batch job and a two-hour staleness limit, the job must run every hour, which the lesson's cost model prices at 24.0 runs per day over 5,000,000 items for $48.50 a day. Two online replicas sized for 120 peak QPS cost $24.00 a day and serve the freshest data. Online wins here; the choice flips when the freshness limit relaxes enough to cut the runs, or when peak traffic grows enough to need many replicas.
questions.full:
### How each plan is priced

| Property | Batch | Online |
|---|---|---|
| Freshness | As old as the last run plus the run time | The data of the request |
| Request latency | One key-value read, a few milliseconds | Feature fetch plus model time, 35 ms in the model |
| Cost driver | Entities times runs per day | Replicas sized for peak QPS, minimum of two |
| New entities | No score until the next run | Scored on the first request |
| When it breaks | Old scores stay readable | Requests fail or time out |

Batch must finish inside the staleness limit, so the time between runs is the limit minus the job time. Each run scores every entity whether or not anyone asks. Online pays for idle replicas between peaks, with a floor of two for availability.

### The arithmetic for this workload

The staleness limit of two hours minus a one-hour job leaves one hour between runs, so 24.0 runs per day. Every run scores all 5,000,000 items. That is why the batch plan costs $48.50 a day while the online plan sits at its two-replica floor of $24.00, since 120 peak QPS fits inside the capacity of two replicas.

### What flips it

- A longer staleness limit cuts runs and batch cost in proportion; the nightly churn job in the same lesson costs under a dollar.
- A staleness limit shorter than one batch job makes batch infeasible at any price.
- A much higher peak needs more replicas and raises online cost linearly with peak traffic.
- A latency budget below the online path's model time rules online out, and a hybrid serves known items from a store and new items online.

### What the decision is not about

Freshness and cost decide; model quality does not change between the two plans. The failure modes differ: a broken batch job leaves old but readable scores, while a broken online service fails requests, so the online design needs a default such as the last stored score or the heuristic.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why is the online plan at its minimum here? Expected: two replicas is the availability floor, and 120 peak QPS fits inside what two replicas handle, so traffic does not drive the count.
- **Level 2:** The job takes longer than the staleness limit. What does the planner return? Expected: infeasible; no schedule satisfies the limit, so the budgets or the job must change.
- **Level 3:** Design the hybrid. Expected: batch scores known items on the relaxed schedule, online scores new items and requests that need fresh data; price it as the sum of a cheaper batch plan and a small online tier.
- **Level 3:** Which design document check does this feed? Expected: the serving-fit check, which prices the chosen mode against the staleness, latency and cost budgets and fails a mode that misses any of them.
questions.wrong:
- "Batch is always cheaper." Batch cost scales with runs per day times entities; a tight freshness limit makes it the expensive plan.
- "Online is always fresher, so always better." Fresher costs replicas, and a nightly process cannot use freshness it does not read.
- "Pick by model accuracy." Accuracy is the same in both plans; the choice is about freshness, latency and cost.

questions.title: Design a chat API for ten thousand daily users
questions.prompt: Design the service behind a chat product with 10,000 daily active users who send about 5 queries each, with roughly 1,500 input tokens and 400 output tokens per query. Users must see a response start quickly, the tail must stay bounded, and the product has a unit cost target. Lay out the request path, the components, the budgets you hold each one to, and how you would scale it.
questions.short: The request enters through a gateway that authenticates and rate limits per user, passes input guardrails, is matched against a semantic cache, and on a miss goes to the model with streaming, then through output guardrails, an eval logger and a cost tracker. The budgets are a median under 2s, a p99 under 10s, a cache hit rate above 30%, a guardrail block rate under 5%, and a cost per request under $0.01. At 50,000 queries a day this runs on a few async servers behind a load balancer; the servers are I/O bound, so a single async process holds a hundred or more concurrent requests and scaling means more servers, not more cores.
questions.full:
### The path

Gateway for authentication, rate limits of 10-50 requests a minute per user and CORS; input guardrails for injection patterns and personal data; a prompt router that picks the template and version; a semantic cache keyed by query embedding with a similarity threshold and a time to live; the model call with streaming and a fallback chain; output guardrails; an eval logger; a cost tracker; a server-sent events response. Seven components, each one a known piece; the engineering is the wiring and the budgets.

### Budgets

| Metric | Target | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Median latency | Under 2s | The typical experience |
| p99 latency | Under 10s | The tail drives churn |
| Cache hit rate | Above 30% | Direct cost savings |
| Guardrail block rate | Under 5% | Higher means false positives |
| Cost per request | Under $0.01 | Unit economics |

Streaming puts the first token inside the median budget even when the full answer takes seconds. Maximum token limits on input and output bound both the cost and the tail. Every external call has a timeout.

### Load and capacity

Traffic is 50,000 queries a day, and with the measured cache hit rate about 32,500 reach the model. Peak matters more than the average; size for the busiest minute. The servers wait on network I/O, so one async process serves 100+ concurrent requests and a box with four workers serves 400+. The lesson's scaling table puts this tier at a few async servers with a cache and a queue, for about $500 a month of infrastructure, with the model bill on top. Connection pooling to the provider avoids a new TLS handshake per request, which costs 100-200ms. Work that is not interactive, such as summarization, goes to a queue with workers and a job id the client polls.

### Observability

Every request writes one structured log line with the request id, the user, the template and version, the model, the input and output token counts, the latency, the cache result, the guardrail results and the cost. Traces across the components show where the time went. The five numbers in the table sit on one dashboard.

### If the model is self-hosted

The pipeline lesson's serving stage adds continuous batching, speculative decoding, and KV cache eviction, with quantized weights for serving and the eval gate rerun on the quantized model. The same gateway, cache and guardrails sit in front of it.

### Before launch

The deployment checklist has fifteen items; the ones people skip are per-user rate limits, maximum token limits, a health endpoint that reports dependency status, timeouts on every external call, and a load test with 100 concurrent users.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** A user pastes a document far longer than the context window. Where is that caught? Expected: at the maximum input token limit before the model call, with a clear error, not at the provider.
- **Level 3:** Why does cost per user matter when cost per request is already under target? Expected: a few heavy users dominate the bill; per-user tracking and a daily cap move them to a cheaper model or stop them.
- **Level 4:** The provider has a regional outage during the daily peak. Walk the request path. Expected: backoff and retries on the primary, fall through the chain to a second model, then cached answers for repeated queries, then an unavailable message; the cost tracker shows the fallback's price and the dashboard shows the step that answered.
- **Level 4:** How do you prove the service meets its budgets before the first user? Expected: a load test at 100 concurrent users against the staging stack with the dashboard metrics as pass criteria, plus a shadow run of the prompts on logged traffic.
questions.wrong:
- "Scale the model servers first." The service is I/O bound at this traffic; the gateway, cache and async servers are the design, and the model is a dependency.
- "Skip the cache; the model is the product." A third of the traffic repeats, and the cache is the largest single saving in the bill.
- "The p99 is a vendor problem." Timeouts, maximum tokens, streaming and the fallback chain are what bound the tail on your side.

questions.title: Design the churn system, not the churn model
questions.prompt: A subscription company with 2,000,000 users wants to reduce churn. The retention team can send a save offer to a small share of users each night. Design the system end to end: the prediction, the decision, the serving mode, the baselines, the rollout, and the failure defaults. State the load and the budgets you assume.
questions.short: The task is binary classification: the probability that a user cancels in the next 30 days, so that the nightly job can pick the top 5 percent for an offer. Nightly scores for every user fit batch inference; the lesson's cost model prices one run a day over the user base at under one dollar, while an online service sized for 40 peak QPS costs $24.00 a day for a freshness nobody needs. The model must beat the idle-days rule by a set lift, ship through shadow and canary stages, and fall back to that rule when anything fails.
questions.full:
### From the goal to a task

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What is predicted, for which entity | Cancellation in the next 30 days, per user |
| Which decision uses it | The nightly job sends an offer to the top 5 percent |
| When is it needed, with which data | Each night, from data up to that night |
| How do we know the decision got better | 30-day churn in the treated group versus a random holdout |

### Load and budgets

Entities: 2,000,000 users. Requests: one score read per user visit. Freshness: a day is fine, because the job runs once a night. Latency budget: one key-value read at request time, a few milliseconds. Cost: the batch plan prices at $0.91 per day for one run over the user base, against $24.00 per day for the minimum two replicas of an online service. A hybrid can score new users online on their first visit, since batch has no score for them until the next run.

### Metrics and baselines

Offline: precision in the top 5 percent. Online: offer acceptance rate and share of users scored. Business: churn in treated versus holdout. Guardrails: offer cost per saved user, unsubscribe rate. Three baselines: majority class, which scores zero on F1 because it never predicts churn; a one-feature idle-days rule fitted on training data; and the current process. In the lesson's demo the model reaches an F1 of 0.564 against the fitted rule at 0.500, a lift of 0.064 above the minimum of 0.02, so the model earns its place. With weaker features the rule would ship instead.

### Data

Labels come from the cancellations table, with a 30-day delay. Every feature must exist at the moment of scoring; a cancellation reason written after the fact leaks the label. Hold out the most recent period for the test split.

### Rollout

Shadow first: score live users, log, never act. Then canary: act for a small share, often 1 to 5 percent, and widen in steps with a rollback switch. Then an A/B test against the holdout for the business metric. Keep the old model deployed and switch traffic by configuration.

### Feedback loop and failures

Offers keep some users, so next month high-risk users look loyal and the retrained model learns that their features do not predict churn. Keep a random holdout that never gets the offer and log the score and the decision with each row. Failure defaults: a failed nightly job serves the last good scores for a fixed time, then the rule; a missing feature takes its documented default and logs; a sudden move in the score distribution pauses automatic offers and alerts a person.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why does the majority baseline score zero? Expected: F1 counts positive predictions, and the majority class is "stays", so there are none.
- **Level 2:** The retention team wants hourly freshness. What changes? Expected: more runs per day raise batch cost in proportion, and the online path becomes cheaper at some point; price both with the cost model.
- **Level 3:** How do you keep the model from learning its own interventions? Expected: a random holdout that never receives offers, plus logging of score and decision so training can separate influenced from clean rows.
- **Level 3:** What is the safe default when the model service is down during the nightly run? Expected: serve the last good scores for a fixed window, then fall back to the idle-days rule.
questions.wrong:
- "Serve it online so scores are always fresh." The decision runs once a night; online replicas cost more for freshness the process cannot use.
- "Use AUC as the offline metric." The decision uses one threshold; precision in the contacted share is the metric that matches it.
- "Retrain monthly on all users." Treated users carry the intervention in their labels; without a holdout the model degrades with each retrain.

questions.title: A spam classifier from 800 messages and a pretrained body
questions.prompt: You have a small pretrained language model and 800 labeled text messages, half spam and half not. Design the classifier: what you keep, what you replace, which of two training regimes you choose, how you split and evaluate, and when the other regime would win.
questions.short: Keep the pretrained body and replace the vocabulary head with a linear layer to two classes over a mean-pooled, mask-weighted sequence vector. With 800 examples, train the head only with the body frozen: it is fast, light on memory and rarely overfits, and on this fixture it reaches about 0.9 precision and 0.85 recall after twenty epochs. Full fine-tuning takes about three times longer and lands within a couple of points either way; it starts to pay off at the scale of 80,000 examples or when the domain drifts far from the pretraining text.
questions.full:
### What to keep and replace

The body already encodes word identity, position and co-occurrence. Training a fresh classifier from scratch on 800 examples throws that away. The head is the wrong part: it projects to the vocabulary. Replace it with one linear layer from the hidden width to two logits over a pooled vector, and train with cross-entropy against the label.

### Pooling

A classifier needs one vector per message. Mean pooling weighted by the attention mask is the simplest stable choice across lengths and needs no special token. The alternatives are a leading class token, which the body would have to be pretrained with, and the last non-padding token, which decoder-style classifiers use.

### Two regimes, one loop

| Regime | Trainable set | Cost | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Head only | The linear head | Fast, almost free in memory | Underfits when the domain is far from pretraining |
| Full fine-tuning | Head and body | About three times longer | Overfits and forgets on small data |

Both run through the same training function; the toggle flips `requires_grad` on the body parameters, so the optimizer sees only the head in the first regime.

### Data and evaluation

Split 80/20, stratified so the test set keeps the 50/50 balance: 640 train, 160 test. Report precision, recall and F1 for the spam class with the confusion matrix, so the numbers can be read as honest estimates. The fixture is balanced and generated, so real data will be noisier.

### The decision

On 800 examples and a tiny body, head only is the right call. On 80,000 examples and a bigger body, full fine-tuning starts to win. A middle path unfreezes only the last block, which costs less than full tuning and learns more than the head alone. The contract is the API, not the winner: one training function, one toggle.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why does the frozen body rarely overfit here? Expected: only the head's few parameters move, so the model cannot memorize 640 examples through the body.
- **Level 2:** Why stratify the split? Expected: so the test set keeps the class balance and precision and recall mean what they say.
- **Level 3:** Precision matters more than recall for this product. What changes in the design? Expected: the decision threshold on the spam logit, chosen on a validation split held out from the 640 training messages to trade recall for precision, so the 160 test messages stay untouched for the final numbers; the training regime stays the same.
- **Level 3:** The messages are in a domain the body never saw. Which regime and why? Expected: full or partial fine-tuning, because the frozen features do not carry the domain and the head alone underfits.
questions.wrong:
- "Train a small classifier from scratch; the model is tiny anyway." That wastes the pretraining and 800 examples are too few to learn the language from zero.
- "Always fine-tune everything for the best accuracy." On small data full tuning overfits and forgets, for a result within a couple of points of the head alone at three times the cost.
- "Use the last token's hidden state without a mask." Padded sequences then pool a padding position; the mask must select the last real token or weight the mean.

questions.title: Accuracy fell and every input monitor stayed green
questions.prompt: A payment model's accuracy, measured as labels arrive, fell from 0.946 to between 0.76 and 0.79. The feature monitors and the score distribution stayed quiet the whole time. The team proposes retraining on the last quarter of labeled data tonight. What happened, why did the monitors miss it, and is the proposal right?
questions.short: The relation between inputs and labels changed while the inputs themselves did not, which is concept drift. Input and prediction monitors compare distributions of features and scores, so a change in the conditional label distribution is invisible to them, and only the outcome monitor can see it, after the label delay. Retraining tonight on the last quarter is the wrong move: most of those labels still describe the old relation, so the model relearns it; collect labels from after the change first, then retrain on them.
questions.full:
### Three kinds of drift

| Drift | What changes | Which monitor sees it |
|---|---|---|
| Covariate | The input distribution | Input monitors |
| Prior | The label rate | Prediction and outcome monitors |
| Concept | The label given the input | Outcome monitors only |

Covariate drift moves features and often leaves accuracy alone. Prior drift moves the positive rate. Concept drift changes which answer is right for the same input, so nothing upstream of the label moves.

### What the demo shows

The lesson's stream injects both kinds. During the covariate segment the PSI and the KS statistic alert on the amount feature while accuracy stays between 0.89 and 0.95. During the concept segment the inputs are identical to the reference, both input monitors stay at their clean values, and accuracy falls from 0.946 to the 0.76 to 0.79 range. The accuracy alert fires 1000 events after the change, and the label delay of 500 events accounts for half of that lag.

### Why the lag

The outcome monitor always looks one label delay into the past, because it can only score the events whose outcome has arrived. The persistence rule, which requires consecutive drift windows before an alert, adds the rest. Both are deliberate: without them the alert rate is unusable.

### Why the retraining proposal is wrong

Retraining answers covariate drift into regions with little data. Concept drift needs labels from after the change. A quarter of labels where the change happened late in the window teaches mostly the old concept. The right sequence is: confirm the change point from the outcome monitor, gather enough labels past it, retrain on those, test on the most recent labeled slice, roll out through shadow and canary, and reset the reference window to the new training data.

### What to do tonight

Route more cases to review if the business impact is large, as a temporary measure while labels from after the change arrive. A threshold move is the lesson's action for prior drift. For concept drift it helps only when the boundary moved on the same score, and it cannot restore a risk order that changed. Keep the model; replace it only with labels that describe the new relation.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Which signal could you add that reacts before the labels? Expected: none for pure concept drift; a proxy such as a review queue outcome or a faster partial label is the only earlier signal.
- **Level 3:** How does a performance estimator that uses predicted probabilities behave here? Expected: it assumes the calibration still holds, so it misses concept drift; the lesson notes that such estimators handle covariate shift and not concept drift.
- **Level 4:** How do you choose how many post-change labels are enough? Expected: enough to test the retrained model on a recent held-out slice with a tolerance you set in advance; the test on recent labels is the gate, not a count.
- **Level 4:** After retraining, the input monitors start to alert on the clean reference. Why? Expected: the reference window was not reset to the new training data, so it compares live traffic with an old distribution.
questions.wrong:
- "The feature monitors are broken; nothing changed in the inputs." They worked as designed; the inputs did not change, the labels did.
- "Retrain on everything so the model sees the new pattern." The old labels outnumber the new ones and the model relearns the old relation.
- "Shorten the windows to catch it faster." Smaller windows add noise and false alarms; the lag here comes from the label delay, which windows cannot remove.

questions.title: The signals that a demo has become a product
questions.prompt: You built a small web demo of a model for reviewers. Three months later a colleague asks whether it is "production". How do you tell, and what changes when the answer is yes?
questions.short: A demo serves known people in short sessions from one process. It has become a product when people outside the team use it every week, when someone asks for an uptime target or reports an outage, when users want to sign in or see history, when the weekly model cost is a budget line, or when the input is covered by a contract or a law. At that point the demo moves onto the production stack with authentication, fallback models, tracing, and cost tracking per user.
questions.full:
### The five signals

- People outside your team use it every week.
- Someone asks for an uptime target, or reports an outage.
- Users ask to sign in, save results, or see their history.
- The weekly model cost is a line in a budget.
- The input includes data that a contract or a law covers.

### What changes

| Property | Demo | Product |
|---|---|---|
| Users | Known people, short sessions | Unknown people, daily use |
| State | None | Accounts, history, saved results |
| Availability | Best effort, one process | A written target, replicas, an on-call owner |
| Cost control | One daily usage cap | Per-user quotas and billing |
| Observability | One log record per request | Traces, metrics, and alerts |

### What the demo already had

A good demo already had the small versions of these controls: an input limit, a per-client rate limit, a daily cap, and a log that keeps the input length and not the text. The product stack adds real authentication at the gateway, a fallback model chain for provider failures, traces across the components, and cost accounting per request and per user. The input limit and the log privacy carry over unchanged.

### Why the question matters

The dangerous state is the middle: a demo with product traffic and demo controls. One daily cap does not stop one tenant from using the whole budget, and one process has no replica to take over when it dies.
questions.followups:
- **Level 1:** Which single signal is the strongest? Expected: an outage report, because it means someone depends on the demo and expects availability.
- **Level 2:** The weekly model cost appears in a budget. What control replaces the daily cap? Expected: per-user quotas and billing, so the total is attributed and limited per tenant.
- **Level 2:** Regulated data starts arriving in the input. What must the log do? Expected: keep no input text and no client address, with a retention period and access control on the records.
questions.wrong:
- "It is production when it runs on a server instead of a laptop." Where it runs does not decide; who depends on it does.
- "Add a disclaimer that it is a demo." A disclaimer does not stop traffic, cost or outages.
- "Keep the demo and build the product separately later." The signals mean the demo already carries product risk now.

questions.title: Review an ML design document and name the blockers
questions.prompt: You are the reviewer for ML design documents before any training starts. A team hands you a document for a payment fraud check that proposes batch scoring, where one job takes an hour, with a three-minute staleness limit, reports an offline AUC, lists a majority-class baseline, and has no rollout section. Walk me through your review: the sections you expect, which gaps block, how you score it, and what you tell the team.
questions.short: The document needs nine sections, and six items block a review because each one makes the system unsafe or useless: the decision that uses the prediction, a business metric, a heuristic or current-system baseline, confirmation that every feature exists at prediction time, a shadow or canary stage with a rollback, and a default action for every failure. This document fails at least three of them: the only baseline is trivial, there is no rollout and no rollback, and the serving choice fails the fit check because batch cannot meet a limit of three minutes when one job takes an hour. I send it back with the blocking list first, and I ask for precision at the decision threshold instead of AUC.
questions.full:
### The nine sections

| Section | Question it answers | Blocking item |
|---|---|---|
| Problem | What is predicted, which decision uses it, why rules are not enough | The decision |
| Metrics | Offline, online, business and guardrail metrics | The business metric |
| Baselines | Trivial, heuristic and current-system baselines | A heuristic or current baseline |
| Data | Label source, delay, feature availability at prediction time | No leakage |
| Budgets and serving | Latency, peak QPS, cost, staleness, and the mode that fits | None |
| Rollout | Shadow, canary, A/B and the rollback | Shadow or canary plus rollback |
| Feedback loops | How the model's decisions alter its later training data | None |
| Failure modes | The default action for each failure | A default for every failure |
| Monitoring | What is watched after launch | None |

### Scoring

Each checklist item has a weight, a blocking flag and a check. Blocking items weigh 2. The score is the sum of passed weights over the total, and the verdict is ready for review only when the score reaches 0.85 and no blocking item fails. A document can score high on the non-blocking items and still be sent back on one blocker; that is the point of the flag.

### The serving fit check

This check reuses the cost model. It reads the workload numbers from the document, prices the chosen mode, and fails when that mode misses the staleness limit, the latency budget or the daily cost budget. A batch job that takes an hour cannot meet a limit of three minutes at any price, so a document that says batch with that limit fails the check. For a payment decision made at request time the fit is online, and the document must state the peak QPS and the p99 budget that size it.

### What I tell the team

1. Blockers first: name the action that each score starts; add the rule the fraud team uses today as the heuristic baseline and set the minimum lift; add shadow and canary stages with a configuration rollback; write a default for a timeout, a missing feature, a new card and a sudden score shift.
2. Then the serving section: switch to online, give the budgets, price it.
3. Then the metric: AUC averages thresholds nobody uses; report precision and recall at the approve, review and block thresholds, and name the business metric and the guardrails.
4. Last the feedback loop and the monitoring, which are not blocking but will decide the second quarter.

### Why the review happens before training

Every failure in the churn story at the start of the design lesson happened before training: no decision, stale cadence, a leaked feature, no comparison with the existing rule. A one-page document asks about each, and the review costs a day where the failures cost a quarter.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** The team says the majority baseline is enough since it scores zero on F1. Why is that the wrong baseline? Expected: it is the trivial one and usually weak; the heuristic or current system is the real competitor and the one the lift is measured against.
- **Level 4:** Why does the serving fit check belong in a document review rather than in load testing? Expected: it is arithmetic on stated budgets and prices, so it catches an infeasible design before a line of serving code exists.
- **Level 4:** The document proposes a hybrid serving mode. What does the checker do and what do you do? Expected: the lesson's cost model has no hybrid plan, so the check fails until a hybrid plan is added; ask the team to price the batch and the online parts and add the plan.
- **Level 4:** What is the one non-blocking section you would still refuse to skip for a fraud system? Expected: feedback loops, because blocked payments never get a label and the model drifts toward its own decisions without a clean sample.
questions.wrong:
- "A strong offline metric compensates for a missing rollout." A model with no shadow stage and no rollback reaches users with no way back; that is why rollout blocks.
- "Score the document and pass it at a high enough total." One failed blocker fails the review regardless of the total.
- "Serving mode is an implementation detail for later." The fit check shows batch cannot meet the limit at all, which changes the architecture and the cost.

questions.title: Design monitoring for a payment risk model
questions.prompt: A payment risk model scores every transaction. Labels arrive weeks later as chargebacks. Design the monitoring: what you watch, how you compare windows, which statistics you compute, and how you keep the alert rate low enough that people read the alerts.
questions.short: Monitor four layers: system health, input distributions, prediction distributions, and outcomes once labels arrive. Compare a fixed reference window with sliding current windows, with the Population Stability Index and the two-sample KS statistic for numeric features and a chi-square test with Cramér's V for categorical ones. Alert only when a corrected p-value and an effect size both pass and the condition persists for consecutive windows, and send warnings to a dashboard rather than to a person.
questions.full:
### Four layers

| Layer | Signals | Available | Question |
|---|---|---|---|
| System health | p50 and p99 latency, error rate, throughput | At once | Does the service answer? |
| Inputs | Feature distributions, missing rates, schema, new categories | At once | Does live data look like training data? |
| Predictions | Score distribution, positive rate, share of default answers | At once | Does the model behave as before? |
| Outcomes | Accuracy, precision, calibration, business metric | After the label delay | Is the model still right? |

Only the last layer measures correctness and it arrives late, so the first three are the early warning.

### Windows

The reference is the training data or a hand-checked production period, fixed until retraining. The current window is the last N events or the last T hours, sliding by a step smaller than its size. A small window reacts quickly and scores noise as drift; a large window is stable but late. Seasonality breaks naive windows, so the reference covers a full cycle or each window is compared with the same period of an earlier cycle. The lesson's demo uses windows of 500 events that move by 250, with labels 500 events late.

### Statistics

- PSI over ten reference-decile bins, with shares clipped to a small value so no bin is empty; conventional bands read below 0.1 as stable and above 0.25 as a significant shift, with the caveat that PSI grows with bins and shrinks with sample size.
- KS statistic D as the effect size for numeric features, with its p-value from the effective sample size; with large samples the p-value alone flags gaps nobody cares about.
- Chi-square with Cramér's V for categorical features, which also reacts to a category that appears only in the current window. With few events in a cell the p-value is not reliable, so pool rare categories into one bin before the test.

### Alert policy

With 50 features checked every hour at an alpha of 0.05, about 60 false alarms a day arrive when nothing changed. Four rules keep the rate useful: correct for multiple tests, so a family alpha of 0.01 over two tests gives 0.005 each; require an effect size; require persistence over consecutive drift windows, two in the demo; and separate dashboard warnings from alerts to a person.

### What retraining does

Covariate drift with stable accuracy often needs no action. Covariate drift into regions with little data calls for retraining on recent data. Prior drift calls for recalibration or a new threshold. Concept drift needs new labels first, because retraining on old labels teaches the old concept again.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why fix the reference window instead of sliding it too? Expected: a sliding reference follows the drift and hides it; the reference changes only at retraining.
- **Level 2:** A clean window shows a tiny chi-square p-value. Why is it a warning and not an alert? Expected: the effect size is below threshold, so the policy logs a warning; the p-value alone is not enough.
- **Level 3:** Labels arrive 500 events late. How does the outcome monitor handle that? Expected: it joins labels as they arrive and computes metrics on the labeled part, always looking that far into the past.
- **Level 3:** Which drift stays invisible to this whole design except the last layer? Expected: concept drift, where the inputs do not change and only outcomes reveal the new relation.
questions.wrong:
- "Alert on any p-value below 0.05." With many features and hourly checks that is dozens of false alarms a day and people stop reading.
- "Watch accuracy; it is the only metric that matters." Accuracy arrives after the label delay; input and prediction monitors give the early warning.
- "Retrain on a schedule and skip monitoring." A schedule retrains when nothing changed and waits when something did.

questions.title: Design the gate that decides whether a model ships
questions.prompt: A team trains and aligns models in a multi-stage pipeline and ships the result to serving. Design the evaluation platform that decides whether an artifact is shippable: what it reads, what a gate is, which two gates catch most disasters, how it handles a failed gate, and how a third party replays a decision.
questions.short: The platform reads a manifest that describes the run completely, with a seed, a code revision, and an input and output hash for every stage, and it evaluates numeric gates that were written before the run started. A regression gate holds the new model to the previous one on core benchmarks and catches training bugs; a KL budget gate caps how far the aligned policy drifted from its reference and catches alignment overcooking. A failed gate holds the run for a named reviewer whose override is logged in the manifest, and anyone can replay the decision because the eval report is content-addressed and the eval data hash is part of it.
questions.full:
### What the platform reads

The manifest is the single file that describes the run well enough to replay it: pipeline version, seed, code revision, and per stage a recipe, an input hash, an output hash, wall clock and cost. The output hash of one stage is the input hash of the next, so a corrupted or swapped artifact stops the pipeline before any evaluation. Artifacts are typed: an eval report carries benchmark scores, regression diffs and the hash of the eval data, so a report cannot be confused with a checkpoint or attached to the wrong model.

### Gates

Every gate is a numeric threshold written before training starts, for example a core benchmark at least the baseline plus 0.5, a coding benchmark at least the baseline plus 1.0, a truthfulness benchmark with no drop, a safety refusal rate at most 0.05, a KL from the reference at most 25.0, and a total cost at most 50000. No "looks good" gates and no subjective sign-offs. If every gate passes the artifact is marked shippable; if any fails the run is held.

### The two gates that matter most

- Regression: the new model must be at least as good as the previous one on the core set. This catches training bugs, bad data mixes and broken tokenizers.
- KL budget: the aligned policy must not drift further than a set amount from its reference. This catches alignment that overcooked the model into a narrow behavior.

Every production pipeline has both.

### Contamination

A gate that compares the eval data hash against the training shards by exact match or long n-gram overlap, and fails when the overlap passes a small fraction, keeps a benchmark gain honest. The pipeline lesson's exercise sets that fraction at 0.1% with 13-gram matching.

### Holds, overrides and replay

A held run is a decision point, not a failure. A named reviewer either approves the rollback or overrides, and the override is written into the manifest with the name. Replay works because the manifest, the content-addressed eval report and the eval data hash identify the exact inputs; a teammate on another continent runs the gate against the same hashes and must get the same verdict. Reproducible is not deterministic: weights can differ at the level of small rounding between runs, so replay checks hashes and headline metrics, not bit-identical tensors.

### Where the platform plugs in

The gate runs after evaluation and after quantization, because quantized weights must pass the same thresholds as the full model. The three commands are plan, run and gate; plan is free and catches missing thresholds and stale hashes before any compute is spent.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why must the thresholds be written before the run? Expected: a threshold chosen after seeing the scores is moved to pass the model; a gate is only a gate if it can fail.
- **Level 3:** A change to the eval set invalidates what? Expected: only the ship decision; the eval data hash changes, the report is recomputed, and the training artifacts stay valid.
- **Level 4:** The quantized model passes every gate except the safety refusal rate, which rose slightly. What do you ship? Expected: nothing without a logged override; the gate exists for the serving artifact, and the lesson's recipe keeps safety evals on a higher-precision quantization where deltas matter.
- **Level 4:** How does the platform stop a model trained through the wrong stage from reaching the gate? Expected: typed artifacts and typed stage signatures, so a preference-tuned checkpoint cannot be fed into the supervised path and the mismatch fails at plan time.
questions.wrong:
- "Have a reviewer look at samples and sign off." Subjective sign-offs are not gates; a gate is a number that can fail, and the reviewer's role is the logged override.
- "Rerun training to confirm a result." Pre-training costs weeks; replay checks hashes and metrics against the manifest instead.
- "One benchmark is enough if it is the right one." The regression set and the KL budget catch different failures, and a safety gate catches a third.

questions.title: Design a feature store that keeps training honest
questions.prompt: Design the feature layer for a churn model. Training needs the value of each feature for millions of user and time pairs. Serving needs the latest value for one user in a few milliseconds. Name the parts, explain how a training row gets its features, and show with the lesson's numbers what goes wrong without the right join.
questions.short: One registry holds each feature definition with its entity, window, default, TTL and version, and both paths compute from it. An offline store keeps the full history with event timestamps for training and backfills; a materialization job copies the latest value per entity into an online key-value store with a TTL. A training row takes the latest feature row at or before its label time, inside the TTL. Without that point-in-time join the lesson's demo looks better offline, 0.948 against 0.893, and worse on new data, 0.763 against 0.876, because the newest snapshot leaks the answer.
questions.full:
### The parts

| Part | Job |
|---|---|
| Registry | One definition per feature: entity, source, transformation, window, default, TTL, owner, version |
| Offline store | Full history with event timestamps, read by training and backfills |
| Point-in-time join | Pairs each label with the latest row at or before the label time, dropped if older than the TTL |
| Materialization | Copies the latest values from offline to online |
| Online store | Latest value per entity, read in milliseconds, refuses rows older than the TTL |
| Skew check | Compares logged serving features with the training path for the same entity and time |

### Two readers, one definition

Training asks "what was the value for each of millions of entity and time pairs". Serving asks "what is the value for this entity now". Both read the same definition from the registry; no service keeps a private copy of the transformation. A change creates a new version, and old models pin the version they trained on.

### The join

1. Find the feature rows of the same entity.
2. Keep rows whose event timestamp is at or before the label time.
3. Take the latest of those.
4. Drop it if the label time minus its event time exceeds the TTL.

A naive join on the entity alone returns the newest row for every label. For a churn label, the newest snapshot already counts the quiet days after the label day, so the feature contains the answer. The demo fits a rule on both training sets and tests on later labels: the naive join scores 0.948 offline and 0.763 on new data, the point-in-time join scores 0.893 offline and 0.876 on new data, and the leaked feature moved the threshold from 19 to 53 idle days.

### TTL and defaults

With a TTL of 10 days, a read five days after the last snapshot returns it, and a read 20 days later returns the defaults because the row is too old. The default lives in the registry so both paths fill a missing value the same way.

### Backfills and created time

A new feature has no history, so a backfill runs the definition at each past date and reads only events at or before that date. A backfill run today can still read data that arrived late, so a strict join also checks the created timestamp.

### The skew check

Log a sample of served features and compare each value with the training path for the same entity and time. Report the mismatch rate and the mean absolute difference per feature, and flag a feature above 1 percent mismatch. Three comparisons separate the causes: store read against training join for the whole system, fresh computation against training join for staleness, and a second code path against fresh computation for code differences.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why does the leaked model look better offline? Expected: the feature contains the outcome, so the offline split rewards it; on new data the information is not there.
- **Level 2:** What does the TTL do in the join, and relative to what time? Expected: it drops a feature row too old for the label; the age is measured from each label time, not from the query time.
- **Level 3:** Two teams compute the same feature in two services. Which skew cause is that, and how does the registry remove it? Expected: two code paths; both services call the registry definition instead of their own copy.
- **Level 3:** Fresher serving features turn out to hurt. Why? Expected: the model trained on weekly snapshots, so values up to six days old are what it learned; staleness skew runs both ways.
questions.wrong:
- "Join labels to the feature table on the user id." That returns the newest value and copies the outcome into the input.
- "Fresher features are always better at serving time." The model learned the freshness of its training data; a different age is skew.
- "Snapshots every day remove the problem." Daily snapshots reduce staleness but the join still needs the as-of rule and the TTL.

questions.title: Keep clean data when the model changes its own future
questions.prompt: Three systems retrain monthly on their own production data: a churn model that sends save offers, a fraud model that blocks payments, and a ranking model that orders a feed. Each one gets a little worse after every retrain. Explain the shared cause, design the data layer that prevents it, and say what each training row must carry for the fix to work.
questions.short: Each model's decisions change the data that trains its next version, which is a feedback loop. Offers keep users who would have churned, so high-risk users look loyal; blocked payments never get a chargeback, so fraud disappears from the blocked region; the feed shows only its top items, so only those collect clicks. The fix is to keep data the model did not influence: a random holdout that never receives the intervention, a small share of random decisions, and a log that stores the score and the decision with every row, joined to features as of the decision time so training can separate influenced from clean data.
questions.full:
### Three shapes of the same loop

| System | How the decision hides the label | What the retrain learns |
|---|---|---|
| Churn offers | Offers retain some at-risk users | Their features do not predict churn |
| Fraud blocks | A blocked payment has no outcome | The blocked region looks safe |
| Feed ranking | Only shown items can be clicked | The current top items are the only good ones |

The loop is listed among the main sources of technical debt in production ML systems because it is silent: every retrain looks fine on its own held-out data, which is also influenced.

### The data layer

1. A random holdout group that never receives the intervention. Its outcomes are the clean estimate of the base rate and the clean labels for training.
2. A small share of random decisions on live traffic, for example payments that are not blocked or items shown out of order, so the blocked and unshown regions keep producing labels. The share is sized as the smallest that keeps enough labels from those regions.
3. Logging of the score, the decision and the assignment with every row at decision time.
4. Features joined as of the decision time, with the point-in-time rule from the feature store, so that a row's inputs are what the model saw and not a later snapshot that already reflects the outcome.

### What a training row carries

The entity and the decision time, the features as of that time, the model score, the decision taken, the group it belonged to, the label and the label time. With those fields training can select clean rows, weight influenced rows, or model the decision as a feature. Without the decision and the group, influenced and clean rows are indistinguishable and the loop is invisible.

### Why the feature store is part of it

A naive join on the entity returns the newest feature snapshot for every label, which copies the outcome into the input. The same mistake inside a feedback loop is worse: the newest snapshot also reflects the intervention. The as-of join with a TTL makes each row describe the moment of the decision, and the created timestamp check keeps a backfill from reading data that arrived later.

### Measuring the fix

The holdout gives the business metric: the outcome in the treated group against the holdout group. It also gives the retrain test: evaluate the new model on holdout rows only, so the score is not inflated by the model's own decisions. A model that improves on influenced data and not on the holdout has learned the loop.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why is a time split alone not enough here? Expected: the recent period is also influenced by the deployed model; time ordering prevents future leakage but not intervention bias.
- **Level 4:** The random non-blocking share costs real fraud. How do you argue for it? Expected: as the price of clean labels against the cost of a model that drifts blind; size it to the minimum that keeps enough labeled fraud from the blocked region.
- **Level 4:** How does the exposure loop in ranking differ from the other two? Expected: the label is never collected rather than hidden; random exposure of lower-ranked items is the only way to learn their click rate.
- **Level 4:** A retrain evaluated on the holdout is worse than on the full set. Which number do you trust? Expected: the holdout; the full set rewards the model for agreeing with its own past decisions.
questions.wrong:
- "More training data fixes a drifting model." The new data is influenced; more of it entrenches the loop.
- "A random train and test split shows the real performance." Both halves are influenced; only a holdout that never saw the intervention is clean.
- "Log the decision later from the outcome table." The decision and the assignment must be recorded at decision time, with the features as of that time, or the join leaks the outcome.

questions.title: One command from raw data to a served tuned model
questions.prompt: A team wants to adapt an open model in the 8B class to its own domain and serve it at a measurable cost per million tokens. Design the pipeline so that one command runs it end to end: the stages, the hardware per stage, the data hygiene, the ablations you require, the serving measurements, and what the release must include.
questions.short: Five stages, each with a config file in version control: data preparation with deduplication, a quality filter, personal data scrubbing and a contamination check against the eval sets; supervised fine-tuning for 2-3 epochs on 8xH100 with a cosine schedule and packed sequences; one epoch of preference tuning on 4xH100 with a swept beta; quantization into three formats; and serving with speculative draft heads and autoscaling on queue wait. The deliverable is an ablation table of base, SFT only, SFT plus DPO and SFT plus GRPO on the task benchmarks, serving numbers at batch 1, 8 and 32 with the draft acceptance rate and cost per million tokens, a safety pass rate, and a model card with seeds, configs and commit hashes.
questions.full:
### Stages and hardware

| Stage | What | Hardware in the capstone |
|---|---|---|
| Data | Deduplicate, filter quality, scrub personal data, split with a seed | CPU |
| Contamination check | Near-duplicate hashing of every validation split against the public test sets; reject overlap | CPU |
| SFT | Sharded optimizer, fast attention kernels, packed sequences, 2-3 epochs | 8xH100 |
| Preference tuning | One epoch of DPO on pairs, or GRPO with a verifiable reward; sweep beta | 4xH100 |
| Quantize | Three formats for deployment flexibility; record size and throughput | One GPU |
| Serve | Draft heads for speculation, autoscaling on queue wait | Serving GPUs |
| Eval and card | Benchmark matrix, safety eval, model card | CPU plus eval GPU |

In the capstone's example run the data stage keeps 280k of 300k examples, SFT takes 6h12m and moves validation loss from 1.42 to 1.03, DPO runs 1h40m at a beta of 0.08, the quantized weights are 4.6 GB, and serving shows a draft acceptance rate of 0.74 with a p99 of 126ms at a batch of 8.

### Hygiene is a gate, not a step

The contamination check runs before training and fails the pipeline on overlap. The capstone's exercise leaks a small share of test answers into training and watches a benchmark jump unrealistically; the check is what makes the eval delta believable. The pipeline lesson adds the mechanism: a manifest with an input and output hash per stage, so the SFT stage refuses data that does not match the hash the contamination check approved.

### Ablations are the deliverable

The question the pipeline answers is not whether the model got better but which stage paid for it. Run the eval matrix on the base, on SFT only, on SFT plus DPO and on SFT plus GRPO. The example reports gains of +3.2 on one benchmark and +0.41 on another after the full run. Without the ablation, a regression from preference tuning hides behind the SFT gain.

### Serving measurements

Tokens per second at batch sizes 1, 8 and 32, the acceptance rate of the draft heads, and the cost for each million tokens against a hosted alternative at matched quality. Acceptance measured on the domain data, not generic chat, because the draft heads were trained for the domain and the latency budget depends on it.

### The release

A model card with the data sources and licenses, the training configs, the eval matrix, the safety pass rate, a reproducibility section with seeds and commit hashes, and the quantization deltas. One command reruns the pipeline with identical seeds; the rubric weights reproducibility and data hygiene as heavily as the eval gain.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why does preference tuning need fewer GPUs than SFT? Expected: it runs one epoch on a much smaller set of pairs, and the capstone sizes it at half the SFT hardware.
- **Level 3:** Which stage gets rerun when the safety eval fails on the quantized model? Expected: quantization and serving only; the pipeline lesson's rollback invalidates the failed stage and its descendants.
- **Level 4:** The acceptance rate on domain traffic is far below the number from generic chat data. What does that do to the design? Expected: the latency budget was set on the wrong number; retrain the draft heads on domain data or size serving without the speculation gain.
- **Level 4:** A smaller model with a low-rank adapter matches quality at a tenth of the memory. How does the pipeline change? Expected: the SFT stage swaps to adapter training with the same data and eval gates, and the quantization and serving stages consume the merged weights unchanged.
questions.wrong:
- "Skip the contamination check; the data is internal." Internal data copies public text all the time, and one leaked test set makes the whole eval table meaningless.
- "Report the final model against the base and stop." Without the per-stage ablation nobody knows whether preference tuning helped or hurt.
- "Measure serving at batch one only." Throughput and cost per million tokens come from batched decoding; batch one measures latency, not economics.

questions.title: A payment fraud check inside a hundred milliseconds
questions.prompt: A payment service must approve, review or block each payment within 100 ms, at 400 requests per second at peak. Fraud labels arrive as chargebacks weeks later. Design the system: the task, the serving mode and its sizing, the data and label plan, the rollout, the failure defaults, and the two things that will quietly break it after launch.
questions.short: The task is binary classification of fraud probability with two thresholds that split the score into approve, review and block, served online because the decision needs the data of the request. At 400 requests a second and 50 ms per request about 20 requests are in flight at any moment, so the service is small, and the budget leaves room for a feature fetch plus the model. Chargeback labels come weeks after the payment, so training uses a time split and features that exist at payment time, and the rollout goes shadow, then canary on a small share, with the heuristic rule as the default on timeout. The two quiet failures are the feedback loop, where blocked payments never get a label, and concept drift, where the same basket changes its fraud risk and only outcome monitors see it.
questions.full:
### Task and decision

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Prediction, per entity | Probability that this payment is fraud |
| Decision | Approve, send to review, or block, inside 100 ms |
| When, with what data | At the request, with the payment, the card history and the device |
| Success | Fraud losses down with the approval rate as a guardrail |

### Serving and sizing

Batch cannot serve this: the staleness limit is zero because the payment did not exist a minute ago. Online inference fetches features and runs the model inside the budget. Little's law sizes it: throughput times latency is the number in progress, so 400 requests a second at 50 ms each is 20 requests in flight, far below what two replicas handle. The p99, not the mean, must stay under the budget; a p99 of 100 ms means 99 of 100 requests finish in time.

### Data and labels

Chargebacks arrive weeks after the payment, so the outcome of recent traffic is unknown. Train on a time split with the most recent labeled period held out. Every feature must exist at payment time; anything written after the outcome, such as a dispute flag, leaks the label.

### Rollout

Shadow: score live payments and log, never act; compare latency, error rate and score distribution with the current rule. Canary: act on a small share, often 1 to 5 percent, widen in steps, roll back by configuration when a guardrail moves. Then measure losses against a holdout.

### Failure defaults

- Model times out: apply the heuristic baseline the team already uses.
- A feature is missing or out of range: use its documented default and log it.
- A new card with no history: the rule or the population average.
- The score distribution moves suddenly: pause automatic blocks and page a person.

### The two quiet failures

1. The feedback loop. A blocked payment never gets a chargeback, so the retrained model sees fewer fraud examples from the region it blocks and slowly learns that region is safe. Give a small random share of payments a non-blocking decision and log the score and the action with every row, so later training can tell influenced data from clean data.
2. Concept drift. Fraudsters change tactics, and payments that were safe start to charge back. Inputs look the same, so input monitors stay quiet; only the outcome monitor sees it, and only after the label delay. Prior drift, such as the fraud rate doubling during an attack, shows up earlier in the prediction monitor as a moving positive rate.

### Monitoring

System health at once, inputs and predictions at once, outcomes joined as chargebacks arrive and computed on the labeled part only. Alert policy with effect sizes, a corrected alpha and persistence, so the on-call person reads the alerts.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why does a time split matter more here than a random split? Expected: a random split leaks future tactics into training and overstates performance on the next month's fraud.
- **Level 3:** The review queue grows after launch. Which guardrail caught it and what do you adjust? Expected: the review rate guardrail; move the review threshold, not the model.
- **Level 4:** The random non-blocking share costs real fraud losses. How do you size it? Expected: as the smallest share that keeps enough labeled fraud examples from the blocked region to retrain; price it as the cost of clean data against the cost of a model that drifts blind.
- **Level 4:** Retraining on the last quarter's labels after a tactic change makes the model worse. Why? Expected: concept drift; most of the labels still describe the old relation, so new labels must be collected before retraining helps.
questions.wrong:
- "Precompute fraud scores nightly for every card." The payment did not exist last night; the decision needs request-time data.
- "Retrain weekly on all blocked and approved payments." Blocked payments have no outcome, so the training set drifts toward the model's own decisions.
- "Watch feature drift and you will see the fraudsters change." Concept drift leaves inputs unchanged; only outcomes show it.

questions.title: Project the monthly bill of a chat feature
questions.prompt: A chat feature expects 10,000 daily active users with 5 queries each, about 1,500 input tokens and 400 output tokens per query, at $2.50 per million input tokens and $10.00 per million output tokens. Measured cache metrics give a 35% hit rate. Walk me through the monthly estimate, and say which number you would attack first.
questions.short: The traffic is 50,000 queries a day, and a 35% cache hit rate leaves 32,500 that reach the model. Over 30 days that is $3,656 of input and $3,900 of output, about $7,556 a month, against $11,625 without the cache, so the cache saves about $4,070. Output tokens cost four times more per token, so after the hit rate the output length is the number to attack, with a maximum output tokens limit and tighter prompts.
questions.full:
### The sheet

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| Daily active users | 10,000 |
| Queries per user per day | 5 |
| Input tokens per query | 1,500 |
| Output tokens per query | 400 |
| Input price per million | $2.50 |
| Output price per million | $10.00 |
| Cache hit rate | 35% |
| Effective daily queries | 32,500 |

Input: 32,500 queries a day times 1,500 tokens times 30 days, divided by a million, times $2.50 gives $3,656. Output: the same with 400 tokens and $10.00 gives $3,900. The total is $7,556 a month.

### Why the cache matters this much

The same traffic without caching costs $11,625. A 35% hit rate removes 35% of the model calls, so it removes 35% of the token cost. The cache is an embedding lookup with a similarity threshold and a time to live, so two differently phrased versions of one question return one answer. The hit rate is measured from the cache metrics, not assumed.

### Which number to attack

- Hit rate first: every point of hit rate is a point off the whole bill.
- Output length second: output tokens are priced four times higher than input, and a maximum output tokens limit per template bounds the worst case.
- Input length third: the system prompt and retrieved context sit in every call; a provider-side cache of the fixed prefix and tighter retrieval cut it.
- Model routing last: a smaller model for simple templates cuts the per-token price, with an eval to prove quality holds.

### Where the estimate goes wrong

The averages hide a tail. A few users who paste long documents or run scripts can dominate the bill, which is why the production checklist tracks cost per user and per request, and why the cost alerting exercise moves a heavy user to a cheaper model past a daily threshold. The target in the lesson's dashboard is a cost per request under $0.01.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Which single metric on the dashboard tells you the estimate holds? Expected: cost per request, which combines token counts and prices and has a target under $0.01.
- **Level 2:** The cache hit rate drops to zero after a prompt template change. Why? Expected: the cache key is the query embedding and the response was generated with the old template; stale entries are invalid or the time to live cleared them.
- **Level 3:** How does prompt caching on the stable prefix change the input line? Expected: the system prompt and fixed instructions are billed at a discount when they repeat, so the effective input price per query falls without changing the token count.
- **Level 3:** What does a per-user daily cap protect that a per-request cost target does not? Expected: the total from one heavy user; many cheap requests still sum to a large bill.
questions.wrong:
- "Multiply users by a cost per user from a vendor page." The bill comes from tokens per query, queries per user and the hit rate; each is measured.
- "Caching saves money only on exact repeats." A semantic cache matches similar queries by embedding, which is why the hit rate reaches a third of traffic.
- "Input tokens dominate because there are more of them." At these prices and lengths the output line is larger even though there are fewer output tokens.

questions.title: A churn model with a good AUC that nobody uses
questions.prompt: A data scientist reports a churn classifier with an AUC of 0.91. Three months after launch, nobody on the retention team uses the scores. The algorithm was fine. Name the design decisions that were missing, and say which metric should have been reported instead.
questions.short: The failures happened before training: nobody named the action a score starts, the scores arrived weekly while the team called customers daily, a feature leaked the label through the cancellation reason, and nobody compared the model with the rule the team already used. AUC averages over every threshold including ones never used; the decision was to contact the top 5 percent each night, so the right offline number was precision in that top 5 percent, paired with online, business and guardrail metrics.
questions.full:
### Four layers of metrics

| Layer | When measured | Churn example |
|---|---|---|
| Offline | Before launch, on held-out past data | Precision in the top 5 percent at the offer threshold |
| Online | During launch, on live traffic | Offer acceptance rate, share of users scored |
| Business | Weeks later, with an experiment | 30-day churn in the treated group versus a holdout |
| Guardrail | All the time | Offer cost per saved user, unsubscribe rate, p99 latency |

The layers disagree often. The offline score comes from a past that did not contain the model. The online metric depends on how people react to the decision. The business metric moves slowly and carries noise from everything else in the company. The guardrails must not get worse.

### Pick the offline metric from the decision

The job contacts a fixed share of users, so the metric is the precision of that share. AUC ranks every pair of users, most of which never reach the decision. The rules guide quoted in the lesson puts it first: design the metrics before deciding what the system does.

### Baselines

An F1 of 0.56 is good against a best alternative of 0.30 and poor against a rule that reaches 0.60. Three baselines are needed: the trivial one, a heuristic such as the idle-days rule the support team used, and the current system. The lift is measured against the strongest one, and a minimum lift is set before the results are seen.

### The other three failures

- Freshness: weekly scores for a daily process means the team acted on stale numbers.
- Leakage: a feature written after the outcome contained the answer, so the offline score was inflated.
- Decision: a score with no action attached cannot change a business metric.
questions.followups:
- **Level 1:** Why is a 30-day churn label slow to evaluate? Expected: the label arrives at the end of the horizon, so the business metric lags the launch by at least that long.
- **Level 2:** Which guardrail would catch a model that saves users at any price? Expected: offer cost per saved user.
- **Level 2:** The heuristic baseline beats the model by a small margin. What ships? Expected: the rule, because it is cheaper to run and explain, unless the model clears the minimum lift.
questions.wrong:
- "A higher AUC would have fixed adoption." Adoption failed on freshness, action and trust, not on ranking quality.
- "Business metrics are enough; skip the offline one." The business metric arrives weeks later and is noisy; the offline metric gates the launch.
- "Guardrails are a product concern, not a model concern." A model that moves a guardrail the wrong way is rolled back no matter its offline score.

questions.title: Write the rollback plan before the training run starts
questions.prompt: A twelve-stage training pipeline runs from tokenizer to inference server, and the pre-training stage costs weeks and millions of dollars. Before the run starts you must write what happens when each stage fails. Lay out the plan, explain how the orchestrator computes what to rerun, and say what "reproduce the run" can and cannot promise.
questions.short: Sort the stages by the cost to rerun them: tokenizer, evaluation, quantization and the server are cheap and rerun in hours, supervised tuning and alignment take days, so the base checkpoint is kept and only those stages rerun, and pre-training takes weeks and a budget in the millions, so the plan is the last good checkpoint plus revised downstream stages. The rerun set falls out of the typed, hashed dependency graph: invalidate the failed stage and every descendant. A replay promises the same code, recipe and source data hashes and the same headline metrics, not bit-identical weights or the same output hashes.
questions.full:
### Three cost classes

| Class | Stages | Plan on failure |
|---|---|---|
| Cheap, hours | Tokenizer, eval, quantization, inference server | Rerun |
| Medium, days | SFT, DPO, constitutional refinement | Keep the base model, rerun alignment |
| Expensive, weeks and millions | Pre-training | Last good checkpoint plus revised downstream stages |

Writing this before the run means nobody improvises at four in the morning with an exhausted team.

### How the rerun set is computed

Every stage has typed inputs and outputs, and the output hash of a stage is the input hash of the next. A failure at the SFT stage invalidates it and every descendant: the reward model, the DPO policy, the refined policy, the eval report, the quantized weights and the server, which is stages six through twelve. A failure at quantization invalidates only quantization and the server. The orchestrator reads the graph from the manifest, so the rollback set is computed, not remembered. A change to the tokenizer invalidates everything downstream; a change to the eval set invalidates only the ship decision.

### Why hashes make it safe

Artifacts live in an immutable store addressed by content hash, never by a name such as latest. A partial rerun checks whether each expected output already exists at the right hash and skips the stage if it does. That is also how a partial rollback saves most of the wall clock: stages one through eight stay cached while nine through twelve rerun. The pipeline lesson's exercise measures exactly that saving.

### What reproduce means

Reproducible: the same manifest, code and infrastructure give a checkpoint with equivalent downstream metrics. Deterministic: bit-identical output. Distributed reduce order, kernel nondeterminism and mixed precision rounding make modern training reproducible but not deterministic; weights differ at a level around 1e-5 between runs while the metrics do not move. The cure is to log the input hash, the output hash and the headline metrics per stage. If the code, recipe and source data hashes and the headline metrics match, the run is reproduced even when a weight artifact and the input hashes after it get new values, and a bit-level diff is the wrong debugging tool. The lesson's rule that the input hash, the output hash and the metrics all match holds in full for the stages with deterministic output, such as the tokenizer and the eval data; for a weight artifact, which cannot be bit-identical, the metrics carry the check.

### Budget as part of the plan

The pre-run cost estimate uses six times parameters times tokens for the training compute, divided by peak throughput and utilization, at the rental rate. If the estimate exceeds the cost gate the pipeline refuses to start. After each stage the remaining budget is rechecked, so an overrun in one stage changes the gate for the next instead of being discovered when the money is gone.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why not name artifacts by version string? Expected: two artifacts can share a name and differ in content; the hash is the identity, and a name like latest is a trap.
- **Level 4:** The reward model and the DPO policy both depend on the SFT checkpoint. What can run in parallel and what must wait? Expected: the two can run together after SFT; the refined policy waits for both, and its input hash must be a deterministic combination of both outputs.
- **Level 4:** A corrupted checkpoint is discovered after alignment finished. Which plan applies? Expected: the expensive class; take the last good pre-training checkpoint and rerun the medium and cheap stages, never the full pre-training.
- **Level 4:** A teammate reports that their replay has different weights. Is the run broken? Expected: not by itself; compare the code, recipe and source data hashes and the headline metrics, and only a mismatch there means the run is not reproduced.
questions.wrong:
- "Rerun from the start to be safe." The expensive stage costs weeks; the typed graph tells you exactly which stages are invalid.
- "Keep the latest checkpoint file and overwrite it each step." A mutable name cannot be verified or replayed; content addressing is what makes the rollback set trustworthy.
- "If the weights are not bit-identical, the pipeline is not reproducible." Distributed training is not deterministic; reproducibility is defined on the code, recipe and source data hashes and the metrics.

questions.title: Put a model demo behind a public link safely
questions.prompt: A reviewer and a customer want to try your model from a link, on a phone, without your notebook. Each model call costs money. Design the demo: the input contract, the order of the checks, the controls for a public link, and what the log is allowed to keep.
questions.short: Write the contract first: a string of 1 to 500 characters with no control characters, a model call with a known cost, and an output that includes a JSON error with a hint. Run the checks in order of cost, body size, access token, per-client token bucket, input validation, daily cap, and only then the model call. Return a stable error code with a message, a hint and a request id, and log the route, the status, the latency and the input length with a keyed hash of the client, never the text or the address.
questions.full:
### The contract

| Part | Question | Answer in the lesson |
|---|---|---|
| Input | What type, size and characters | A string of 1 to 500 characters, no control characters |
| Model call | How long and how much | Known latency and cost per call |
| Output | What the user sees on success and failure | A label and a reply, or a JSON error with a hint |

A notebook has no limit on any part. The demo sets one on each, and the server applies it to every client, because any client can skip the page.

### Checks in order of cost

1. Read the content length and refuse a body over 4,096 bytes before reading it.
2. Check the access token when one is required.
