3. Take one token from the client's bucket; refuse with 429 and a `Retry-After` header when empty.
4. Parse and validate the body: JSON object, text present, inside the limit, no control characters, with 422 for a bad field.
5. Charge the daily cap; refuse with 503 and `Retry-After` when the day's budget is spent.
6. Call the model.

A bad request stops at the first failed check and costs almost nothing. The paid step is last, so only valid requests count against the cap.

### Controls once the link is public

| Risk | Control |
|---|---|
| One client floods | A token bucket per client: a capacity for bursts, a refill rate for the long run |
| Strangers find the link | An optional access token in the authorization header |
| Total cost grows | A daily usage cap over all clients, counted in windows of 86,400 seconds |
| Large or odd input | Body limit, text limit, control character check |
| Logs keep private input | Records with the input length and a keyed hash of the client |

A rate limit controls each client and not the total; a hundred polite clients can still spend the budget, which is what the cap is for.

### Errors a user can act on

Every error has the same shape: a stable `code` for clients and tests, a `message` with the numbers the user needs, a `hint` with one action, and a `request_id` that joins a user report to one log record. A stack trace does none of these jobs for a stranger.

### Feedback and streaming

The page disables the button while a request runs, shows the elapsed time, and shows the time to first token when it arrives, so the user can tell a slow model from a broken page and does not click again. Tokens stream as server-sent events over a POST body, not a GET URL, so the input never lands in an access log.

### What the log keeps

Route, status, error code, latency and input length, plus a keyed hash of the client address for per-client counts. Never the input text, never the raw path, never the address. The page tells users what is kept.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why does the daily cap run after validation and not before? Expected: so only valid requests count against the budget; a rejected request should not spend it.
- **Level 2:** Behind a reverse proxy every request has the proxy's address. What breaks? Expected: all users share one bucket; read the client address from a header that only your proxy sets and trust it from nowhere else.
- **Level 3:** Why send the input in a POST body instead of the URL for the event stream? Expected: servers and proxies write URLs into access logs, so a GET would store user text.
- **Level 3:** A framework builds the page for you. Which controls are still your job? Expected: the rate limit, the cost cap and log privacy; the frameworks save work on the form and the streaming, not on the risks of a public link.
questions.wrong:
- "Validate in the browser with a maximum length attribute." The browser helps honest users only; the server repeats every check.
- "A rate limit per client is enough to control cost." It bounds each client, not the sum; the daily cap bounds the total.
- "Log the full request so you can debug reports." The log then holds user text and addresses; a request id joins a report to a record without either.

questions.title: Design cited search over ten repositories of code
questions.prompt: An engineering organization wants to ask questions across 10 repositories with about 2M lines of code and get answers that cite file and line. The index must stay fresh on every push. Design the ingestion, the retrieval, the answer step, the freshness path, and the evaluation, with the budgets you would commit to.
questions.short: Parse each file into function and class nodes and chunk at those boundaries, give each chunk a dense embedding, sparse terms and a one-sentence summary, and store a graph of imports and calls between chunks. A query runs dense and sparse search in parallel, merges and deduplicates, reranks the top 50 with a cross-encoder to keep 10, and hands those to a long-context model that must cite every claim by file and line; uncited claims are dropped. A push triggers a symbol-level diff so only changed chunks re-embed, with a budget of under 60 seconds for a 50-file push. Quality is measured on 100 labeled cross-repo questions with MRR@10, nDCG@10, citation faithfulness and p50 and p99 latency.
questions.full:
### Ingestion

- A push webhook starts a worker that collects the changed files.
- A parser with grammars for the languages in the fleet extracts function and class nodes with their full source span. Chunks follow node boundaries, not fixed token windows.
- Each chunk gets three representations: a dense code embedding, sparse terms in a field-weighted index with symbol names weighted 4, bodies 1 and summaries 2, and a one-sentence summary written by a small model with the system preamble cached.
- A symbol graph records imports, calls and inheritance across files and repositories, used at query time to expand retrieval across repo boundaries.

The summary is the third retrievable modality: a user asks how something is authorized, the code says `check_permission`, and the summary says authorization.

### Retrieval and answer

1. Fire dense and sparse search in parallel, deduplicate by repository, path and symbol.
2. Rerank the top 50 with a cross-encoder and keep the top 10.
3. Call the synthesizer with the reranked chunks and a cached system prompt, requiring a file and line anchor on every claim.
4. Parse the output and check each anchor against the span at the indexed commit; a claim without an anchor, or with a span that is missing or does not support it, is re-asked or dropped. Only verified claims return.

Naive cosine search alone is poisoned by generated boilerplate, monorepo duplication and rarely imported symbols, which is why the hybrid search, the reranker and the graph exist.

### Freshness

On each webhook compute the symbol-level diff. Re-embed only the chunks whose text changed, recompute the import, call and inheritance edges of the changed symbols, and delete the chunks, summaries and edges of removed files and symbols from every store. The budget is a 50-file push searchable in under 60 seconds for the whole fleet, without reprocessing the 2M lines.

### Evaluation and budgets

| Weight | Criterion | Measure |
|---|---|---|
| 25 | Retrieval quality | MRR@10 and nDCG@10 on 100 held-out questions |
| 20 | Citation faithfulness | Share of claims with a verifiable file and line anchor |
| 20 | Latency and scale | p95 query latency at 10k QPS on the indexed corpus |
| 20 | Incremental indexing | Time from push to searchable on a 50-file commit |
| 15 | Answer formatting | Clickable citations, snippet previews, follow-up affordance |

A weekly rerun of the 100 questions with an alert on an MRR@10 drop above 5% catches drift in the index or the models.

### The service around it

The query path sits inside the production stack from the application lesson: a gateway with per-user limits, guardrails on input and output, streaming of the answer, structured logs per retrieval and synthesis step, and cost tracking that attributes the summary model, the embeddings, the reranker and the synthesizer separately.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why chunk at syntax nodes instead of fixed token windows? Expected: a window cuts functions in half and mixes neighbors; a node is one coherent unit with a stable symbol name to cite and deduplicate on.
- **Level 3:** What does the reranker add that the two retrievers cannot? Expected: it scores each query and candidate pair together, which is more accurate than cosine on separate embeddings, at a cost that only the top 50 can afford.
- **Level 4:** Generated boilerplate makes up a fifth of the corpus. What happens and what do you change? Expected: retrieval poisoning, where near-duplicate generated code crowds the results; flag generated chunks in the payload and down-weight them.
- **Level 4:** A question needs code from four repositories. Which component carries that? Expected: the symbol graph expands the candidate set across import and call edges, so the reranker sees chunks from repositories the first search missed.
questions.wrong:
- "A million-token context window replaces retrieval." Context helps but does not rank; cross-repo questions still need retrieval and citations.
- "Dense embeddings alone are enough for code." Exact symbol names need the sparse index, and the summary catches intent that the code text does not state.
- "Re-index the fleet on every push to keep it simple." Reprocessing 2M lines per commit blows the freshness budget; the diff keeps the index consistent at a fraction of the work.

questions.title: Offline accuracy was fine and live accuracy is not
questions.prompt: A churn model scored well offline and does worse than the older, simpler model on live traffic. Serving features are computed by another team's service. You have a sample of logged serving requests. Design the triage: which comparisons you run, in which order, what each one isolates, and what the fix looks like for each cause you find.
questions.short: Compare the same entity and time across three pairs. The online store read against the training join tests the whole system and should show zero skew when both read one definition. A fresh computation against the training join isolates staleness, and the second team's code path against a fresh computation isolates code differences such as window boundaries and defaults. Each pair gives a mismatch rate and a mean absolute difference per feature, and the fix for every cause is the same shape: one registry definition that both paths call, with logged serving features checked against it.
questions.full:
### The four causes

| Cause | What happens | Example from the lesson |
|---|---|---|
| Two code paths | Training and serving compute the feature differently | The serving window includes one extra day |
| Stale features | The served value has a different age than training saw | Training read weekly snapshots, serving computes fresh |
| Different defaults | The two paths fill a missing value differently | Training used 365 for no purchase yet, serving used -1 |
| Time travel | Training read a value from after the label time | A naive join took the newest snapshot |

### The three comparisons

1. Online store read against the training join. Both read the same materialized rows from one definition, so every feature should show a mismatch of zero. A nonzero result here means the store or the join itself is wrong.
2. Fresh computation against the training join. This isolates staleness. In the lesson's demo the fresh value differs on most requests: 83.0% mismatch for days since last purchase, 30.5% for the purchase count, 37.1% for spend. Fresher is not better here, because the model learned from values up to six days old.
3. Second code path against fresh computation. This isolates code. The demo shows 12.5% mismatch on both window counts, because the other team's window includes one extra day, and 5.5% mismatch on days since last purchase with a mean difference of 20.07, which comes only from new users where the defaults disagree, -1 against 365.

The check needs the same request keys on both sides, and it fails loudly when the keys differ or when there are no requests, because a missing request hides skew and an empty check proves nothing.

### The fixes

- Two code paths: delete the private copy; both services call the registry definition, and a change creates a new version that old models do not pick up.
- Stale features: match the serving age to the training age, or retrain on the fresher snapshots; a feature's freshness is part of its definition.
- Different defaults: one default in the registry, applied by one function in both paths.
- Time travel: the point-in-time join with the TTL, which the demo shows moves offline accuracy from an inflated 0.948 to an honest 0.893 and live accuracy from 0.763 to 0.876.

### Why the simpler model won live

The older model used features that both paths computed the same way. The new model trusted a feature whose live values came from a different window and a different default, so it saw inputs it never trained on.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Which comparison would you run first with one hour available? Expected: the first one; if the store read matches the training join, the system is consistent and the problem is elsewhere, and if not, every downstream check is moot.
- **Level 3:** The defaults differ only for new users. Why does the mismatch rate understate the damage? Expected: the rate is low because new users are few, but the difference per mismatch is huge, so the model's output for every new user is wrong.
- **Level 4:** The other team cannot change their service this quarter. What do you do? Expected: log their served features, train the next model on those logged values so training matches serving, and keep the skew check running so the gap is visible.
- **Level 4:** How does a created timestamp enter the triage? Expected: a backfill written today can read late-arriving data, so a strict join also drops rows created after the label time; otherwise the training path itself is skewed.
questions.wrong:
- "Fresh serving features are always better than training snapshots." The model learned the training freshness; a different age is skew in either direction.
- "A mismatch rate under a few percent is fine." A small rate with a large mean difference, as with the defaults, still breaks every affected prediction.
- "Compare offline accuracy with live accuracy and call it drift." Drift is a change over time; skew is a difference between two readers of the same feature at the same time, and the three comparisons tell them apart.

questions.title: Keep a chat service answering when the provider does not
questions.prompt: Design the request path of a chat service that calls a hosted model. Users leave when nothing appears for a few seconds, the provider returns rate limits and server errors at night, and the vector store behind retrieval sometimes times out. Cover what the user sees, how you retry, and what happens when each part fails.
questions.short: Stream tokens over server-sent events so the first token appears in a few hundred milliseconds even though the full answer takes seconds. Retry provider failures with exponential backoff and jitter, capped at three retries, then fall through an ordered chain of models to a cached answer and finally a short unavailable message. Secondary systems degrade instead of failing the request: no retrieval context when the vector store is down, a direct model call when the cache is down, and a clear message when a guardrail blocks.
questions.full:
### Streaming

A response of a few hundred output tokens takes 3-8 seconds to finish. Without streaming the user watches a spinner for all of it. With streaming the first token arrives in 200-500ms, the total time is the same, and the perceived latency drops. Server-sent events are the default: one direction, over plain HTTP, consumed by the browser's event source or any HTTP client. Websockets are for two-way needs such as voice, and long polling is for clients that cannot do either.

### Three layers of failure

| Layer | Example | Recovery |
|---|---|---|
| Provider | 429 rate limit, 500 server error, timeout | Backoff with jitter, then the fallback chain |
| Model | Malformed JSON, invented function name | Retry once with the error in the prompt |
| Application | Vector store slow, cache down, guardrail exception | Degrade: skip the secondary system |

Backoff starts at one second, doubles on each attempt and adds random jitter so that many clients do not retry in step. Three retries is the cap; after that the request moves to the next model. Every external call has a timeout, with a default around 30s.

### The fallback chain

Primary model, then a cheaper or more available model, then a smaller one, then a cached response, then the unavailable message. Each step trades quality for availability. The user always gets something, and the log records which step answered so the cost tracker and the quality dashboard can attribute it.

### Degradation table

- 429: retry with backoff; queue the request and tell the user it is processing.
- 500: retry up to three times, then switch model; transparent to the user.
- Timeout: one retry with a shorter prompt or a smaller model.
- Malformed output: retry with the error attached, else return the raw text.
- Guardrail block: no retry; explain why the request was blocked.
- Vector store down: no retry on the store; answer without retrieval context.
- Cache down: no retry on the cache; call the model directly.

### The user-visible contract

The dashboard targets are a median under 2s and a p99 under 10s. Streaming moves the first-token time inside the median target even when the full response does not. A streamed response has one trap: the status line is sent before the first token, so a failure after that must be sent as an error event inside the stream.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why add jitter to the backoff? Expected: many clients that fail at once would otherwise retry at the same instants and reproduce the overload.
- **Level 2:** Why is a guardrail block not retried? Expected: the input is the problem; retrying the same input gives the same block and spends a call.
- **Level 3:** The fallback model has a different price. Where does that show up? Expected: in the cost tracker per request and per model, so the dashboard shows the cost of the outage, not only its rate.
- **Level 3:** The stream has started and the model fails. What can the server still do? Expected: send an error event inside the stream, because the HTTP status is already committed.
questions.wrong:
- "Retry until the provider answers." Unbounded retries pile up during an outage; cap them and fall through the chain.
- "If retrieval is down, fail the request so the answer stays grounded." A secondary system must not take down the primary flow; answer with reduced context and log it.
- "Buffer the whole response and send it at once for simplicity." The user sees nothing for seconds and leaves; the total time is the same either way.

questions.title: When to say no to a model
questions.prompt: A product owner asks your team for "a model" to decide which support tickets get escalated. Before you design anything, what questions decide whether this should be a learned model at all, and what would make you answer with a rule instead?
questions.short: I ask whether a short rule already reaches the goal, whether labels exist or can be collected, whether anyone will act on the prediction, whether the data at decision time holds the signal, and whether one error is acceptable. A model loses when a few conditions stay correct and explain themselves, when there are no labels, or when the cost of building and running the system exceeds the value of the better decisions. A model wins when the rule has grown long and fragile, because a learned model is easier to update than a complex heuristic.
questions.full:
### The cases against a model

| Condition | Why a rule wins |
|---|---|
| The logic fits in a few conditions and stays correct | Cheaper to run, test and explain |
| No labels and no practical way to collect them | Nothing to learn from |
| Nobody acts on the prediction | A better score changes nothing |
| The decision-time data does not contain the signal | The model cannot see what matters |
| One error is unacceptable and no person checks the output | A probabilistic system will be wrong sometimes |
| The system costs more than the better decisions are worth | Negative return |
| The problem changes faster than retraining | The model is always stale |

A lookup table or a threshold that covers 99% of cases is the right system, and adding a model raises maintenance cost for little gain.

### The cases for a model

The rules guide quoted in the design lesson says not to fear launching without machine learning, and also to prefer a model over a complex heuristic. The crossing point is when the rule has many branches, breaks on new cases, and nobody can say why it decides as it does. A learned model is retrained; a long rule is rewritten.

### How I would run the ticket case

1. Ask what the escalation decision is, who makes it, and when the features exist.
2. Build the rule the support team already uses, even if it lives in a spreadsheet, and measure it.
3. Set the minimum lift a model must show over that rule before any training.
4. Only then collect labels and train, and compare against the rule with the same metric.

The rule is also the safe default when the model service fails, so it is built first either way.
questions.followups:
- **Level 1:** Where do labels for ticket escalation come from, and what is their delay? Expected: from past escalation decisions or outcomes, which arrive after the ticket closes; the delay sets how fresh the training data can be.
- **Level 2:** The team has no escalation history at all. What do you build first? Expected: the rule, with logging of the decision and its inputs, so labels start to accumulate.
- **Level 2:** A regulator requires that every escalation decision be explainable. What changes? Expected: either keep the rule or restrict the model to interpretable forms such as a small tree or a linear model.
questions.wrong:
- "A model always beats a rule given enough data." The rule can win when the features carry weak signal, and the lift must be measured, not assumed.
- "Collect data later; ship the model first." Without labels there is nothing to train on and nothing to evaluate against.
- "The heuristic baseline is just a sanity check." It is the real competitor and the safe default for failures.
